The proposed answer of 371 is correct.

**Lower bound.** The condition says every pair of cities has at least 2 common neighbours.

- A vertex v of degree 2 with neighbours a and b has at most one common neighbour with a (namely b), so the minimum degree δ is at least 3.
- Counting the 2(n−1) required common-neighbour incidences at a minimum-degree vertex v gives Σ_{w∈N(v)} (d_w − 1) ≥ 2(n−1). Hence Σ_{w∈N(v)} d_w ≥ 2(n−1) + δ.
- The n−1−δ vertices outside N[v] each have degree at least δ. So 2m ≥ δ + (2(n−1)+δ) + δ(n−1−δ) = 2(n−1) + δ(n+1−δ).
- For δ = 3 this is 5n−8. For larger δ up to n−1 the bound is at least as large when n ≥ 6, since δ(n+1−δ) is concave in δ and is larger than 3(n−2) at δ = 4 and at δ = n−1. Small n do not matter here, since the sum starts at n = 10.
- So m ≥ ⌈(5n−8)/2⌉.

**Construction.** Take two hubs adjacent to each other and to every other vertex, giving 2n−3 edges. Add a perfect matching on the n−2 non-hubs, or a matching plus one path of length 2 (three vertices) if n−2 is odd. This adds ⌈(n−2)/2⌉ edges, and every non-hub then has a partner.

- Two non-hubs have both hubs as common neighbours.
- A hub and a non-hub have the other hub and the non-hub's matching partner as common neighbours.
- The two hubs have all n−2 non-hubs as common neighbours.

The total is 2n−3 + ⌈(n−2)/2⌉ = ⌈(5n−8)/2⌉, which matches the lower bound.

**Sum.** The values of S(n) for n = 10 to 20 are 21, 24, 26, 29, 31, 34, 36, 39, 41, 44, 46. Their sum is 371.
